name: reject-prototype-name
description: An unlock request carrying contentNames that are inherited member names in JavaScript. THE ATTACK. sealed.contentKeys carries "constructor" and "__proto__", each holding a genuine sealed blob of this render. On the wire they are two ordinary strings, since a contentName is whatever the publisher called a field. In JavaScript, map["constructor"] answers out of Object.prototype with a function rather than missing, "__proto__" read on a plain object reaches the prototype chain, and "__proto__" WRITTEN on one moves the prototype instead of adding a member. WHY THE REQUEST IS REFUSED WHOLE. The identifier grammar is letter-initial, so "__proto__" is not a name any consumer admits, and the format says a map keyed by identifiers is rejected whole when one member name violates that grammar rather than having the invalid name skipped beside its siblings. The issuer admits every request identifier before policy, BIND construction or private-key work, so this body is a whole-request binding_failed refusal: no key, no per-coordinate error, and the private key untouched. "constructor" is a different case and the grammar admits it - it is letter-initial and carries no reserved character - which is why it travels here beside the name that is refused. WHAT THIS VECTOR PINS BESIDE THE REFUSAL. Every map that comes off the wire is keyed by a name the client chose, so core/IssuerEngine.js and ports/UnlockEndpoint.js read them with Object.hasOwn or off Object.keys (and the port's status table is a Map, for the same reason). The response side is the same hazard pointed the other way: an issuer that builds its errors map or its keys map by plain assignment writes a prototype instead of a member for "__proto__", and a coordinate can then go back unreported. Identifier admission closes the request path to that name, and the map-building discipline is what keeps a runtime difference from appearing anywhere else, since PHP has no prototype chain and both names are unremarkable array keys there. NOT CONFORMANT: a TypeError or a 500 anywhere in the pass; a key of any kind; a 200 carrying either name in keys or in errors; a response map whose prototype was moved. Note JSON.parse makes both names OWN properties of the parsed object, so the refusal is a rule about the name and not a lookup accident. REPLAY. Post `rawBody` VERBATIM - the string as it sits in this file, never a re-serialization of it - to the unlock endpoint, with `issuer` as the key material the issuer holds for its own name and keyId, and `publisher.signingKeys` as the public verification halves, read straight from this file rather than resolved by a deployment lookup. A pass is: expected.code where there is one; key material back for exactly the coordinates in expected.keys and no others; and an error back for exactly the coordinates in expected.errors, under the codes recorded there. No publisher private key is in this file, on purpose: an issuer never holds one, so everything a reject vector asks for is checkable with what a real issuer has. HOW FAR THE REFUSAL REACHES IS PART OF WHAT IS PINNED, and expected.privateKeyReached says which side of the line this body lands on. A request that fails integrity - a signature that does not verify, a signed resource with no renderId to bind to - has asked nothing that could be answered, so it is refused whole and before the key store is consulted at all. A blob presented at a coordinate it was not sealed at is one bad blob in an ordinary request: the only way to find out is to try it, so the key store is reached, the blob comes back as an error, and everything else the request carried is answered beside it. The untouched coordinates were never the attack, and a page has to keep working around one bad blob, so they are answered. Everything in the body but the attack is the render this vector was cut from - the envelope, the periodKeys section and the untouched blobs are what the publisher emitted. An unchanged regeneration retains the valid resourceJWT signature segment inside rawBody, so the body is byte-stable with seal-ecdh.json. A fresh seal still draws a new k, which is why a replayer verifies the segment rather than comparing it. The token is the one in the base vector from the same run, byte for byte, except in reject-no-renderid, reject-renderid-noncanonical and reject-renderid-wrong-width, whose envelopes are second tokens signed over resources with the renderId removed, given a noncanonical spelling, or resized, which is each vector's whole subject; in reject-forged-resourcejwt, whose signature segment was drawn by a key the publisher does not hold; in reject-tampered-resourcejwt, which carries the seal-ecdh token's own signature segment under a payload edited after signing; and in the two reject-alg-substituted arms, which carry that token's payload segment under a header rewritten to name another algorithm, with a third segment that is empty or a MAC - neither of which moves between runs.
